subject: science
title: Build a Mini Ecosystem
objective: Explain how organisms depend on each other in a small ecosystem.

visual.title: Mini ecosystem image
visual.caption: A model showing sun, plants, insects, soil, water, and a simple food connection.

teachingSupport.summary: An ecosystem is a set of living and nonliving parts that depend on each other.
teachingSupport.description: Learners build a model, add dependency arrows, remove one part, and explain how the system changes.

diagramCallouts.title: Energy source
diagramCallouts.body: Sunlight starts many food connections because plants use it to make food.

diagramCallouts.title: Dependency arrow
diagramCallouts.body: An arrow means one part needs or affects another part.

diagramCallouts.title: System change
diagramCallouts.body: Removing water, plants, or insects changes more than one part of the ecosystem.

helperNotes: Sort cards into living and nonliving before drawing arrows.
Ask what each part needs to survive.
Use a missing-part challenge to test whether the learner understands relationships.

commonMisunderstandings.mistake: Thinking only animals are important in an ecosystem.
commonMisunderstandings.fix: Trace how plants, sunlight, water, and soil support the animals.

commonMisunderstandings.mistake: Drawing arrows as decoration instead of relationships.
commonMisunderstandings.fix: Require every arrow to be read aloud as depends on or gives to.

teachingSupport.confusionPrompt: Write whether you are stuck on living parts, nonliving parts, arrows, or what changes when one part disappears.

funTasks: Build a paper mini ecosystem with arrows that show who depends on what.
Play dependency Jenga: remove one part and explain what changes.
Act out sun, plant, insect, and decomposer roles in a tiny ecosystem loop.
reward: Unlock the Ecosystem Builder badge after explaining a new ecosystem.

sections.warmup: Name three living or nonliving parts of a backyard or park.
sections.teach: Organisms depend on food, water, shelter, sunlight, and other organisms. A model can show these connections.
sections.guidedPractice: Connect plants, insects, water, soil, and sunlight with dependency arrows.
sections.independentPractice: Explain what might happen if one part of the ecosystem disappears.
sections.activity: Build a mini ecosystem model with labeled arrows.
sections.reteach: Separate living and nonliving parts, then ask what each part needs.
sections.challenge: Compare a pond ecosystem and a garden ecosystem.

quiz.prompt: Why do many plants need sunlight?
quiz.explanation: Plants use sunlight as part of making their food.

quiz.prompt: What does a dependency arrow show in an ecosystem model?
choices: How one part depends on another
quiz.explanation: Dependency arrows show relationships between parts of a system.

studentFacing.mission: Build a tiny ecosystem and prove how each part helps the system stay alive.
studentFacing.whyItMatters: Science is about relationships. When one part changes, other parts can change too.
studentFacing.bigIdea: Living and nonliving parts form a system when they depend on each other.
modelSteps: Sort each part as living or nonliving.
Draw arrows for needs or effects.
Remove one part and predict what changes.
studentFacing.example: A plant uses sunlight and water; an insect may use the plant for food or shelter.
studentFacing.nonExample: An arrow with no explanation is decoration, not science evidence.
studentFacing.quickCheck: Read every arrow out loud as 'depends on' or 'gives to.'
studentFacing.studentSummary: An ecosystem is a web of parts that need or affect each other.
studentFacing.tutorHandoff: Tell the tutor if the confusing part is living/nonliving, arrows, or what changes when one part disappears.

learningObjective: Explain how organisms depend on each other in a small ecosystem.
successCriteria: I can describe the big idea in Build a Mini Ecosystem.
I can use a visual model or example to solve a new problem.
I can explain my reasoning and repair a misunderstanding.
I can retrieve and transfer the idea after a delay.
essentialQuestion: How can a model help us explain what changes in a living system?

knowledge: An ecosystem is a set of living and nonliving parts that depend on each other.
capability: Explain how organisms depend on each other in a small ecosystem.
Use a model, example, or explanation to demonstrate the idea.
reasoning: Use evidence from the model or task to justify a choice.
retention: Retrieve the core idea after the original lesson context is removed.
transfer: Apply the idea to a new example, context, or problem.

phaseModules.title: Notice the challenge
phaseModules.studentAction: Look at the model and describe what you notice about Build a Mini Ecosystem.
phaseModules.visualSupport: Build a tiny ecosystem and prove how each part helps the system stay alive.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can say what I am trying to figure out before I choose an answer.

phaseModules.title: Build a model
phaseModules.studentAction: Organisms depend on food, water, shelter, sunlight, and other organisms. A model can show these connections.
phaseModules.visualSupport: Energy source: Sunlight starts many food connections because plants use it to make food.
phaseModules.successCheck: My model shows the important parts and how they connect.

phaseModules.title: Spot the parts
phaseModules.studentAction: Sort the examples, evidence, or steps that belong to Build a Mini Ecosystem.
phaseModules.visualSupport: Dependency arrow: An arrow means one part needs or affects another part. System change: Removing water, plants, or insects changes more than one part of the ecosystem.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can explain why one choice fits and another choice does not.

phaseModules.title: Try the method
phaseModules.studentAction: Connect plants, insects, water, soil, and sunlight with dependency arrows.
phaseModules.visualSupport: A plant uses sunlight and water; an insect may use the plant for food or shelter.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can use the model to complete a new example.

phaseModules.title: Explain the why
phaseModules.studentAction: Read every arrow out loud as 'depends on' or 'gives to.'
phaseModules.visualSupport: An arrow with no explanation is decoration, not science evidence.
phaseModules.successCheck: My explanation names evidence or a rule, not only an answer.

phaseModules.title: Show your thinking
phaseModules.studentAction: Explain what might happen if one part of the ecosystem disappears.
phaseModules.visualSupport: Choose a drawing, spoken explanation, labeled model, or written response.
phaseModules.successCheck: Another learner could understand my reasoning from my proof.

phaseModules.title: Retrieve it later
phaseModules.studentAction: After a short delay, recall the key idea from Build a Mini Ecosystem without copying the original example.
phaseModules.visualSupport: An ecosystem is a web of parts that need or affect each other.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can retrieve the idea when the order and example change.

phaseModules.title: Use it somewhere new
phaseModules.studentAction: Compare a pond ecosystem and a garden ecosystem.
phaseModules.visualSupport: A new context, example, or problem that keeps the same underlying idea.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can recognize when this idea is useful outside the original example.

phaseModules.title: Choose your next move
phaseModules.studentAction: Tell the tutor if the confusing part is living/nonliving, arrows, or what changes when one part disappears.
phaseModules.visualSupport: Pick a helper note, alternate model, reteach path, or challenge path based on your evidence.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can name what is still confusing and choose a productive next step.

proofTasks.prompt: After a delay, retrieve the key idea from Build a Mini Ecosystem.
Read every arrow out loud as 'depends on' or 'gives to.'
Explain what might happen if one part of the ecosystem disappears.
Complete a delayed Memory Vault check for Build a Mini Ecosystem.
Compare a pond ecosystem and a garden ecosystem.

feedbackRules.result: Thinking only animals are important in an ecosystem.
feedbackRules.hint: Trace how plants, sunlight, water, and soil support the animals.
feedbackRules.action: Route to the alternate representation before retrying.

feedbackRules.result: Drawing arrows as decoration instead of relationships.
feedbackRules.hint: Require every arrow to be read aloud as depends on or gives to.
feedbackRules.action: Route to the alternate representation before retrying.

reteachPaths.trigger: The learner misses the model or cannot explain the key relationship.
reteachPaths.action: Separate living and nonliving parts, then ask what each part needs.

prerequisiteRepairPaths.trigger: The learner cannot identify the basic parts needed for the lesson.
prerequisiteRepairPaths.action: Use a short sort, match, or vocabulary check before returning to the main task.

challengePaths.trigger: The learner completes the proof independently.
challengePaths.action: Compare a pond ecosystem and a garden ecosystem.

parentTeacherNotes: Treat independent transfer and delayed recall as stronger evidence than one immediate quiz score.
accessibilityNotes: Provide text, visual, oral, and keyboard-accessible ways to demonstrate understanding.
Do not rely on color alone.
